sentences.t: ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησ’ Ἑλένη Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα·
sentences.l: Then again another thing devised Helen, sprung of Zeus;
sentences.i: Then, in her turn, Helen, the daughter sprung from Zeus, thought of something else;
sentences.n: ἐνόησ’ is ἐνόησε, the aorist of νοέω ’perceive, devise’, and it IS augmented: the initial ἐ- is the augment and stands in plain sight. What is elided is a different vowel — the verb’s own final -ε, dropped before the following vowel-initial Ἑλένη (whose Ἑ- itself carries a rough, not smooth, breathing). This line echoes the fixed formula ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη, with Ἑλένη Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα, ’Helen, sprung of Zeus’, standing in for Athena; ἐκγεγαυῖα, a perfect participle of ἐκγίγνομαι, follows the wording already fixed for Ἀργείη Ἑλένη, Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἄρ’ εἰς οἶνον βάλε φάρμακον, ἔνθεν ἔπινον,
νηπενθές τ’ ἄχολόν τε, κακῶν ἐπίληθον ἁπάντων.
sentences.l:
At once then into the wine she threw a drug, from which they drank,
grief-easing and anger-easing, a forgetting of all ills.
sentences.i: At once she threw into the wine they were drinking a drug that eased grief and eased anger, bringing forgetfulness of every trouble.
sentences.n: βάλε is the unaugmented second (thematic) aorist of βάλλω, on the bare stem βαλ-: Attic ἔβαλε simply prefixes the augment to this same stem, so this is exactly the same phenomenon as πάθεν, ἴδεν, φύγον and τέκε — an ordinary past tense without the ἐ- — not an athematic root aorist like ἔβην or the augmented κατέδυ seen below. νηπενθές (νη- privative + πένθος ’grief’) and ἄχολον (ἀ- privative + χόλος ’bile, anger’) describe the drug itself; ἐπίληθον governs the genitive κακῶν ἁπάντων, ’causing forgetfulness of all ills’. This is the poem’s famous nepenthe.

sentences.t:
ὃς τὸ καταβρόξειεν, ἐπὴν κρητῆρι μιγείη,
οὔ κεν ἐφημέριός γε βάλοι κατὰ δάκρυ παρειῶν,
sentences.l:
whoever should gulp it down, when it had been mixed in the bowl,
would not, for that day at least, let a tear fall down his cheeks,
sentences.i: whoever swallowed it down, once it had been mixed into the bowl, would not shed a single tear the whole day through,
sentences.n: καταβρόξειεν and βάλοι are optatives in a generalizing conditional clause, so the question of augment does not arise for them (the optative never takes one). ἐφημέριος (ἐπί + ἡμέρα) is ’lasting a day, for that day’, a rare word. The sentence that begins here runs five lines to a period at 226; it is cut here, at the comma after παρειῶν, because a period would otherwise run past four lines, and the syntax pauses most strongly at exactly this point, before the two οὐδ’ εἴ clauses begin.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ εἴ οἱ κατατεθναίη μήτηρ τε πατήρ τε,
οὐδ’ εἴ οἱ προπάροιθεν ἀδελφεὸν ἢ φίλον υἱὸν
χαλκῷ δηιόῳεν, ὁ δ’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ὁρῷτο.
sentences.l:
not even if his mother and father had died,
not even if before his face his brother or dear son
with the bronze they should slay, and he with his own eyes should see it.
sentences.i: not even if his mother and father had died, not even if before his eyes they killed his brother or dear son with the bronze, and he watched it happen.
sentences.n: κατατεθναίη is a perfect optative of θνῄσκω (reduplicated stem τεθνα-); δηιόῳεν is a present optative of δηϊόω ’slay’ with its contracted -οῖεν artificially stretched to -όῳεν, the same diectasis seen in αἰτιόωνται. ὁρῷτο is a present optative of ὁράω. None of these carries an augment, since the optative mood is never augmented; that issue concerns only indicative past tenses, such as ἐνόησε above.

sentences.t:
τοῖα Διὸς θυγάτηρ ἔχε φάρμακα μητιόεντα,
ἐσθλά, τά οἱ Πολύδαμνα πόρεν, Θῶνος παράκοιτις
Αἰγυπτίη, τῇ πλεῖστα φέρει ζείδωρος ἄρουρα
φάρμακα, πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ μεμιγμένα πολλὰ δὲ λυγρά·
sentences.l:
Such cunning drugs the daughter of Zeus possessed,
good ones, which to her Polydamna gave, Thon’s consort,
the Egyptian, whose grain-giving plough-land bears the most
drugs, many good mixed in and many baneful;
sentences.i: Such cunning drugs the daughter of Zeus possessed, good ones that Polydamna, the wife of Thon, had given her, an Egyptian woman whose grain-giving plough-land bears the most drugs of all, many good ones mixed in among many harmful;
sentences.n: Διὸς θυγάτηρ keeps the house rendering ’the daughter of Zeus’ already fixed for Athena, used here of Helen. ζείδωρος ἄρουρα, ’the grain-giving plough-land’, is the phrase already fixed at 3.3, where an ancient alternative reading, ’life-giving’ (from ζάω), is also on record beside the usual ’grain-giving’. μητιόεντα (from μῆτις) describes the drugs as ’cunning, subtly wrought’. Πολύδαμνα and Θῶνος are proper names otherwise unknown to the poem, an Egyptian couple; παράκοιτις is simply ’bedfellow, wife’. πόρεν is an unaugmented second (thematic) aorist (πορ-), the same unaugmented pattern as βάλε above and not, strictly, a root aorist, beside Attic ἔπορεν.

sentences.t:
ἰητρὸς δὲ ἕκαστος ἐπιστάμενος περὶ πάντων
ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.l:
and each physician is skilled beyond all
men;
sentences.i: and every physician there is skilled beyond all other men;
sentences.n: ἐπιστάμενος is a present participle standing with an unexpressed ἐστί (’each physician is skilled’), and it takes the genitive περὶ πάντων ἀνθρώπων, ’beyond all men’ — the same superiority-with-genitive idiom seen in περὶ… ἐστὶ βροτῶν of Odysseus. The unit ends mid-line 232, at the raised point after ἀνθρώπων, and the rest of that line opens the next unit.

sentences.t: ἦ γὰρ Παιήονός εἰσι γενέθλης.
sentences.l: for indeed they are of the race of Paieon.
sentences.i: for they are indeed descended from Paieon.
sentences.n: Παιήων (here genitive Παιήονος) is a distinct healing god, older than and separate from Apollo Paean; the two are not the same figure in Homer. γενέθλη is ’stock, race, offspring’. The claim is that Egyptian physicians as a class descend from this god’s line, which explains their famous skill with drugs.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἐνέηκε κέλευσέ τε οἰνοχοῆσαι,
ἐξαῦτις μύθοισιν ἀμειβομένη προσέειπεν·
sentences.l:
But when she had put it in, and bidden them pour the wine,
once more with words, answering, she addressed them:
sentences.i: But when she had put it in and told them to pour the wine, she spoke to them again in these words:
sentences.n: ἐνέηκε, from ἐνίημι, keeps the verb’s own long root vowel rather than adding a separate augment; κέλευσέ has no augment at all (Attic ἐκέλευσε). προσέειπεν is the uncontracted, still-augmented form of προσεῖπε (προσ-έ-ειπε), left unfused because Homer still feels the lost digamma of the root Ϝεπ-. This line closes the narration of the drug and opens Helen’s second speech of the visit.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη Μενέλαε διοτρεφὲς ἠδὲ καὶ οἵδε
ἀνδρῶν ἐσθλῶν παῖδες·
sentences.l:
“Atreus’ son, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, and you as well,
the sons of noble men;
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, and you too, the sons of noble men;
sentences.n: The line adapts the fixed vocative Ἀτρεΐδη Μενέλαε διοτρεφές, ὄρχαμε λαῶν to a different continuation: here Helen also addresses the young men present, οἵδε…παῖδες, ’you here, the sons of noble men’ — Telemachus and Peisistratus. Quotation marks open here (English layers only; Murray prints none) for this new speech, and they are not closed anywhere within this slice.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ θεὸς ἄλλοτε ἄλλῳ
Ζεὺς ἀγαθόν τε κακόν τε διδοῖ·
sentences.l:
but the god — to one now, to another now —
Zeus gives both good and bad;
sentences.i: but the god Zeus gives good and evil, now to one man, now to another;
sentences.n: ἄλλοτε ἄλλῳ is a distributive idiom, ’at one time to one man, at another to another’, governing διδοῖ, uncontracted for δίδωσι. The claim generalizes what Zeus himself said about mortals blaming the gods for troubles they bring on themselves.

sentences.t: δύναται γὰρ ἅπαντα·
sentences.l: for he is able to do all things;
sentences.i: for he has power over everything;
sentences.n: δύναται takes ἅπαντα as a bare object (understood as ‘to do’), and the half-line simply restates, as a general reason, the claim just made about Zeus’s unlimited power to give both good and bad.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι νῦν δαίνυσθε καθήμενοι ἐν μεγάροισι
καὶ μύθοις τέρπεσθε·
sentences.l:
Now indeed you feast, sitting in the halls,
and in stories take delight;
sentences.i: Now you are feasting, seated in the halls, and taking your pleasure in stories;
sentences.n: δαίνυσθε and τέρπεσθε are present middle imperatives-cum-descriptions addressed to the diners; μύθοις is an instrumental dative, ’with stories’. μεγάροισι is a dative plural in -οισι(ν) for a single hall, as often.

sentences.t: ἐοικότα γὰρ καταλέξω.
sentences.l: for fitting things I shall tell in order.
sentences.i: for I will tell a tale that fits the occasion.
sentences.n: ἐοικότα, ’fitting things’, is a neuter plural object of καταλέξω, a future of καταλέγω ’recount in order’, the verb regularly used in this poem for formal storytelling.

sentences.t:
πάντα μὲν οὐκ ἂν ἐγὼ μυθήσομαι οὐδ’ ὀνομήνω,
ὅσσοι Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονός εἰσιν ἄεθλοι·
sentences.l:
All things I could not tell, nor could I name them all,
as many as are the trials of Odysseus the enduring-minded;
sentences.i: I could not tell everything, nor name it all, all the trials that steadfast Odysseus underwent;
sentences.n: μυθήσομαι and ὀνομήνω are futures (the second an aorist-subjunctive-shaped form with future sense) governed by οὐκ ἄν, a modest disclaimer before the single story Helen will actually tell. ταλασίφρονος keeps the fixed rendering ’enduring-minded’ / ’steadfast’ already used of Odysseus.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οἷον τόδ’ ἔρεξε καὶ ἔτλη καρτερὸς ἀνὴρ
δήμῳ ἔνι Τρώων, ὅθι πάσχετε πήματ’ Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
But such a thing this strong man did and dared
in the land of the Trojans, where you suffered woes, you Achaeans.
sentences.i: But this strong man did and dared such a thing in the land of the Trojans, where you Achaeans suffered woes.
sentences.n: καρτερὸς ἀνήρ, ’the strong man’, is plain and not yet house-fixed. Line 243 is word-for-word the same line already published in odyssey-009 (Telemachus’s plea to Nestor, = 4.243/329); its shipped English, ’in the land of the Trojans, where you suffered woes, you Achaeans’ / ’…in the land of the Trojans, where you Achaeans suffered woes’, is reused here verbatim, with only the terminal punctuation changed from comma to period to match this unit’s grammar.

sentences.t:
αὐτόν μιν πληγῇσιν ἀεικελίῃσι δαμάσσας,
σπεῖρα κάκ’ ἀμφ’ ὤμοισι βαλών, οἰκῆι ἐοικώς,
ἀνδρῶν δυσμενέων κατέδυ πόλιν εὐρυάγυιαν·
sentences.i: He disfigured himself with degrading blows and threw foul rags about his shoulders, and looking like a household slave, made his way into the wide-streeted city of his enemies;
sentences.n: δαμάσσας and βαλών are unaugmented aorist participles (no participle ever takes the augment). κατέδυ, by contrast, IS augmented: it is κατά + ἔδυ, the root aorist of δύω ’sink, enter’, with the augment ε- fused inside the tmesis compound; the same verb recurs, still augmented, at 249. εὐρυάγυιαν (εὐρύς + ἄγυια ’street’) is kept distinct from the already-fixed εὐρυόδεια ’wide-wayed’ (of earth), a different noun.

sentences.t:
ἄλλῳ δ’ αὐτὸν φωτὶ κατακρύπτων ἤισκε,
δέκτῃ, ὃς οὐδὲν τοῖος ἔην ἐπὶ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
and as another man, concealing himself, he made himself seem,
a beggar, who was nothing such among the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: He disguised himself and made himself look like someone else, a beggar, quite unlike what he really was among the ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἤισκε is the augmented imperfect of (ἐ)ίσκω ’make like, liken’ — the η- is the augment on an original ε-, not a separate long vowel, and is easy to mistake for an unaugmented form. δέκτης, ’beggar, one who receives’, is from δέχομαι.

sentences.t:
τῷ ἴκελος κατέδυ Τρώων πόλιν, οἱ δ’ ἀβάκησαν
πάντες·
sentences.l:
Like to him he went down into the city of the Trojans, and they
were all astonished;
sentences.i: Looking just like that beggar, he made his way into the city of the Trojans, and everyone was astonished;
sentences.n: κατέδυ repeats the augmented aorist of 246. ἀβάκησαν, by contrast, is unaugmented: its ἀ- belongs to the verb’s own stem (privative ἀ- + the root of βάζω ’speak’, literally ’were struck speechless’), not a dropped temporal augment — Attic would lengthen a true augment here to η-.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δέ μιν οἴη ἀνέγνων τοῖον ἐόντα,
καί μιν ἀνηρώτων·
sentences.l:
but I alone recognized him, being such as he was,
and I questioned him;
sentences.i: but I alone recognized him for what he really was, and questioned him;
sentences.n: ἀνέγνων (ἀνα-έγνων) and ἀνηρώτων (ἀνα-ἠρώτων) are both augmented — the augments ἐ- and ἠ- are fused inside the tmesis compounds and easy to overlook. οἴη, ’alone’ (feminine), marks that only Helen, of all the Trojans, saw through Odysseus’s disguise.

sentences.t: ὁ δὲ κερδοσύνῃ ἀλέεινεν.
sentences.l: but he by his craftiness evaded me.
sentences.i: but with his native cunning he evaded me.
sentences.n: ἀλέεινεν is unaugmented (from ἀλεείνω ’avoid, shun’; Attic would lengthen the initial α- to η- under the augment). κερδοσύνη, ’craftiness, cunning’, is built on the same root as κέρδεα οἶδεν, already used of Odysseus’s stock cleverness.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή μιν ἐγὼ λόεον καὶ χρῖον ἐλαίῳ,
ἀμφὶ δὲ εἵματα ἕσσα καὶ ὤμοσα καρτερὸν ὅρκον
μὴ μὲν πρὶν Ὀδυσῆα μετὰ Τρώεσσ’ ἀναφῆναι,
sentences.l:
But when I bathed him, and anointed him with oil,
and put garments about him, and swore a mighty oath
not to reveal Odysseus among the Trojans,
sentences.i: But when I had bathed him, anointed him with oil, and put clothes on him, and had sworn a solemn oath not to reveal that this was Odysseus among the Trojans,
sentences.n: λόεον and χρῖον are unaugmented imperfects (λόω ’wash’, χρίω ’anoint’); ἕσσα is the unaugmented aorist of ἕννυμι ’clothe’; ὤμοσα is the augmented first-person aorist of ὄμνυμι ’swear’. The correlative μὴ… πρίν… πρίν γε, ’not… before… until’, is split across the unit boundary here, forced by the four-line cap, and is completed in the next unit.

sentences.t:
πρίν γε τὸν ἐς νῆάς τε θοὰς κλισίας τ’ ἀφικέσθαι,
καὶ τότε δή μοι πάντα νόον κατέλεξεν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
not until he had reached the swift ships and the huts,
then at last he told me all the plan of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: not until he had reached the swift ships and the huts, only then did he tell me the whole plan of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἀφικέσθαι completes the πρίν γε clause begun in the previous unit. κατέλεξεν, ’recounted, told in order’, is the same verb Helen used of her own coming narration at 239 (καταλέξω): the disguised beggar and the storytelling queen are both, in this passage, tellers of ἐοικότα.

sentences.t:
πολλοὺς δὲ Τρώων κτείνας ταναήκεϊ χαλκῷ
ἦλθε μετ’ Ἀργείους, κατὰ δὲ φρόνιν ἤγαγε πολλήν.
sentences.l:
And many of the Trojans having killed with long-edged bronze,
he came back among the Argives, and brought back much knowledge.
sentences.i: And after killing many Trojans with the long-edged bronze, he made his way back to the Argives, bringing back a great deal of intelligence.
sentences.n: φρόνις, ’knowledge, intelligence’ (built on the root of φρήν), is a rare noun found only here in Homer and is kept plain rather than folded into any already-fixed φρήν-compound. ταναήκεϊ χαλκῷ, ’with the long-edged bronze’, combines ταναός ’long, stretched’ with ἀκή ’point, edge’.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ἄλλαι Τρῳαὶ λίγ’ ἐκώκυον·
sentences.l: Then the other Trojan women wailed shrilly;
sentences.i: Then the other Trojan women raised a shrill wail;
sentences.n: ἐκώκυον IS augmented: κωκύω begins with a consonant, so its imperfect takes the ordinary prefixed syllabic augment ἐ- (unaugmented would be the bare κώκυον), the verb specifically for a woman’s shrill ritual wail, distinct from ordinary weeping. The other Trojan women’s grief here is set directly against Helen’s private relief in the lines that follow.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμὸν κῆρ
χαῖρ’, ἐπεὶ ἤδη μοι κραδίη τέτραπτο νέεσθαι
ἂψ οἶκόνδ’, ἄτην δὲ μετέστενον, ἣν Ἀφροδίτη
δῶχ’, ὅτε μ’ ἤγαγε κεῖσε φίλης ἀπὸ πατρίδος αἴης,
sentences.l:
but my heart
rejoiced, since already my spirit had turned to return
back home, and I mourned over the blindness which Aphrodite
gave, when she led me there, away from my dear fatherland,
sentences.i: but my own heart rejoiced, since by then my spirit had turned toward returning home again, and I lamented the blindness that Aphrodite had given me, when she led me there, away from my dear fatherland,
sentences.n: τέτραπτο is a pluperfect passive of τρέπω, ’had been turned’; κραδίη and κῆρ, both simply ’heart’, stand one right after the other for two different Homeric words for the same organ. ἄτη is the ruinous blindness or delusion a god sends, here laid at Aphrodite’s door as the cause of Helen’s abduction; δῶχ’ is δῶκε, an unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι.

sentences.t:
παῖδά τ’ ἐμὴν νοσφισσαμένην θάλαμόν τε πόσιν τε
οὔ τευ δευόμενον, οὔτ’ ἂρ φρένας οὔτε τι εἶδος.
sentences.l:
forsaking my daughter, and my chamber, and my husband,
a man lacking in nothing, neither in mind nor at all in looks.
sentences.i: abandoning my daughter, my marriage chamber, and my husband — a man who lacked nothing, neither in understanding nor in looks.
sentences.n: νοσφισσαμένην is an aorist middle participle, ’having forsaken, parted from’, agreeing with the speaker’s own remembered self. δευόμενον, ’lacking’, takes the genitive τευ (= τινός); φρένας is an accusative of respect. Helen’s speech, opened with a quotation mark at 235, is NOT closed anywhere in this slice: it runs on without a break past line 264, and is closed only when Menelaus replies at 4.265 in the next slice.
